title: Pipeline priming variability scratchpad
content:
Quick note: capturing an ad-hoc set of runs exploring how pipeline priming/warm paths affect tail latency and throughput when request sizes vary and when payloads arrive with jitter. Purpose is to decide whether a small proactive KV-cache + staged pipeline priming step is worth shipping as an opt-in heuristic for Dedicated fleets.

Context / hypothesis
- Observed sporadic p99 spikes during short-duration, high-concurrency blends on small models (7B-ish). Hypothesis: pipeline stages (pre- and post- tokenization, CPU->GPU copies, attention kv cache warmup) are not fully amortized for mixed short/long request sets; initial requests incur asymmetric overheads.
- Goal: quantify the magnitude of the extra latency and its decay curve, and measure throughput loss when we add thin priming requests.

Experiment harness
- Runner: lightweight harness using k6 (http2/1.1), plus native gRPC runner for the production RPC surface.
- Model: open-7b-llama-variant (quantized int8), context length 1024.
- Nodes: 4x A10G-equivalent in Dedicated pool, pinned to same region, NVLink enabled for larger nets.
- Config toggles: batching=on/off, kv_cache=true/false (fresh vs persistent), prologue priming request of n tokens (0/8/32), pipelined CPU prefetch (on/off).
- Arrival profiles: Poisson lambda=50 rps, Poisson lambda=200 rps, deterministic burst 500rps for 2s every 30s, and a mixed small/large payload mix (70% 32-token, 30% 512-token).
- Measurement: per-request latency histogram, GPU occupancy sampled via nvidia-smi every 1s, throughput and dropped requests. 5x repeats per condition.

Raw summary numbers (median across repeats):
- Baseline (no priming, batching on, persistent kv): Poisson 200 rps, p50=45ms, p95=120ms, p99=260ms, throughput sustained 190rps
- Coldpath (no priming, kv disabled between requests): p50=75ms, p95=230ms, p99=520ms, sustained 150rps
- Priming 8 tokens (light prologue before client request): p50=46ms, p95=115ms, p99=250ms, sustained 188rps
- Priming 32 tokens: p50=48ms, p95=118ms, p99=245ms, sustained 185rps
- Priming + prefetch CPU (best combo): p50=44ms, p95=110ms, p99=230ms, sustained 192rps

Observed decay curve (single short sequence after idle): overhead measured relative to steady-state baseline
- Request 1 after idle: +180ms median overhead (NVMe->GPU, kernel jit, first allocation)
- Request 2: +60ms
- Request 3: +20ms (near steady)
- After 8 requests: within 5% of steady p50

Notes on variance
- Mixed payload runs show larger p99s: short requests interleaved with long ones suffer from KV-cache churn and context swap costs; p99 up to 2x baseline in worst mix.
- Burst experiments: deterministic 2s 500rps bursts cause queueing and batching contention leading to p95 increase by ~1.8x vs Poisson at same average rate. Short bursts create a transient GPU occupancy drop (observed as <50% for ~1.2s) due to driver-level scheduling and CUDA context warmup.

Key micro-observations
- CPU prefetch (pre-parsing + tokenization) reduces first-request penalty significantly for small payloads; it's cheap (single-threaded tokenization). We can push tokenization slightly off the critical path.
- Very small priming prologue (8 tokens) recovers ~90% of the benefit of 32-token priming while adding minimal cost to throughput.
- Persistent KV cache is the single biggest win, but it's costly for memory when there are many concurrent contexts. Consider partial persist for top-k tenants.
- Batching on is necessary for throughput; but it amplifies p99 during bursts unless we cap batch window size.

Quick cost/benefit mental model
- Priming adds ~1-2ms average per request if injected always; but if we only inject on suspected cold paths (heuristic: idle > 3s or first request after context swap), cost becomes negligible vs p99 reduction.
- Implementing an opportunistic priming sampler (1 in N cold requests) gives asymmetric benefit: reduces p99 tail without >5% throughput hit.

Actionable next steps (short)
- Implement prototype: lightweight priming prologue with configurable token-count (default 8), gated by idle-time heuristic and tenant opt-in flag.
- Add server-side tokenization prefetch path as an async prefetch for small requests.
- Create A/B test on Dedicated pool with 10% traffic for two weeks; monitor p99, error-rate, GPU mem pressure.
- Add telemetry: mark primed requests in traces, capture delta-first-request latency metric.

TODOs / questions
- TODO: instrument kernel launch times to confirm if CUDA JIT is dominant for first request on new model variant (ENGINF-3421 assigned). Owner: Arjun.
- Question: memory overhead for partial persistent KV per-tenant — simulate with 2000 concurrent small contexts. Lina to run mem-only simulation.
- TODO: Add a guard that skips priming when model is currently saturated to avoid increasing tail on spikes.

Hypothesis for productization
- Make priming an opt-in Dedicated feature with default off for Hosted until we have tighter memory/throughput safety checks. Could be a toggle in the Route config (priming: none|opportunistic|always).

Notes to self
- Keep experiment scripts in the repo under /bench/pipeline-priming/ — need to push later. Capture seed and run ids.
- Slack thread: ping #eng-serving-runtime with brief results and propose A/B test.

References / links
- ENGINF-3421 (profiling kernel launch times)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/789 (proto for priming toggle)
- Slack: https://slack.com/archives/C02ABCDEF/p1700000000000

Final quick takeaway
- Small, targeted priming (8 tokens + CPU prefetch) gives most of the tail reduction benefit with minimal throughput impact. Worth prototyping and running a limited A/B in Dedicated.
